sentences.text: The premaxillae bore four slender, unserrated teeth, the second of which was the largest.
Behind these, the maxilla carried roughly fifteen additional unserrated teeth.
Altogether the animal possessed about twenty teeth, with the anterior teeth narrow and close together and the posterior teeth broader and more widely spaced.
Nine cervical vertebrae are preserved in the holotype, although ten are inferred to have been present.
The forelimb measured about sixty percent the length of the hindlimb, indicating relatively long arms.
Feathers along the tail base and central tail region measured between twenty and thirty millimetres in length.
Feathers on the femur and tibia ranged from twenty-five to thirty-five millimetres, reaching up to sixty millimetres on the metatarsals.
The femur bowed forward and was shorter than the tibia, a condition seen in several theropods.
Impressions of a keratin sheath surround the hand and foot claws, preserving details of the outer covering.
Large wing-like membranes covered the forelimbs, while the hindlimbs bore shorter wings.
The enlarged claw on the second toe measured seven and a half millimetres, with an additional four and a half millimetres contributed by a keratin sheath.
Body feathers over the head and neck varied from ten to thirty-five millimetres in length.
Approximately sixteen long feathers were visible at the tip of the tail, resembling those of early avialans and some scansoriopterygids.
Fossils of Changzhousaurus were recovered from the Jiufotang Formation in western Liaoning Province, China.
The holotype individual was not a juvenile, yet it had not yet reached full maturity at death.
According to Xu (2026), it occupies a basal position within Deinonychosauria, supporting the monophyly of that clade.
The species lived during the Early Cretaceous Aptian stage.
Its age is constrained between 121.4 and 113.2 million years ago.
Paleontologists continue to debate whether dromaeosaurids and troodontids together form a single monophyletic group called Deinonychosauria.
